svg.aria-label: Four periods, 2000 to 2026, across five tracks: motive and money, attackers, operating system, internet, security products. Every event is a dot with its date on hover; the anchor events are labelled; the four period bands light up one at a time
svg.font-family: Inter, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Four periods, 2000 to 2026, across five tracks: motive and money, attackers, operating system, internet, security products. Every event is a dot with its date on hover; the anchor events are labelled; the four period bands light up one at a time

circle.title: 2000 · Notoriety — Early-2000s worm authors seek fame rather than money.
2000 · VBScript worms (first script wave) — ILOVEYOU, May 2000; Anna Kournikova, February 2001. Macro viruses had led the way since 1995.

2000 · Outlook blocks executable attachments — Outlook E-mail Security Update, June 2000; mail gateways follow. Office 2000 macro security levels end the first script wave. Attackers answer by diversifying file types.
2000 · Signature antivirus — File scanners and signature databases.
2000 · Plaintext HTTP — HTTPS only for login and payment.
2000 · Mass-mailing worms — Executable attachments and self-mailing worms.
2001 · IE6 and ActiveX — Internet Explorer 6 dominance.
2001 · Code Red, Nimda — Code Red, July 2001 (IIS, MS01-033); Nimda, 18 September 2001: worms that spread over the network with no email and no user action.
2001 · Windows XP — Released 25 October 2001: users run as administrator, autorun on, firewall off by default.
2002 · Packers and protectors — UPX (1998), ASPack, Armadillo; Themida 1.0 in December 2004.
2003 · Heuristics and emulation — Scanners run the file a little to see through packers.
2003 · Slammer — 25 January 2003: one UDP packet exploiting SQL Server (MS02-039), spreading worldwide in minutes.
2003 · Adware, pay-per-install — Infected machines monetized through installs and ads.
2003 · Broadband replaces dial-up — Always-on hosts; email as the delivery channel.
2003 · Blaster — 11 August 2003: exploits the RPC DCOM flaw (MS03-026) on Windows 2000 and XP; Windows XP SP2 turns the firewall on the next year.

2003 · IRC botnets: Agobot, rxbot — 2002–2004: Agobot (Gaobot), SDBot and its rxbot derivatives make the compromised machine join an IRC channel and take orders. Infections become inventory, rented for spam, DDoS and installs.
2004 · Hacker Defender — Windows user-mode rootkit; v1.00 released January 2004.

2004 · Mass-mailers switch to zip (MyDoom, Bagle) — MyDoom, 26 January 2004, mails itself in zip archives; Bagle.F, 29 February 2004, in password-protected zips, the password shown as an image by mid-March. The answer to attachment blocking, within weeks.
2004 · HIPS, anti-spam, VirusTotal — Host intrusion prevention; VirusTotal launched 2004.
2004 · Sasser — 30 April 2004: exploits the Windows logon service, LSASS (MS04-011), with no user action; Windows XP SP2 ships with the firewall on that August.
2004 · Gmail blocks executables, zips included — Documented by June 2004: messages with executable attachments, even inside zip archives, bounce to the sender. Gmail adds .js in February 2017.
2004 · DDoS extortion, DDoS for hire — Botnets flood online businesses for ransom and are rented out for attacks; Ancheta indicted for selling botnet access for DDoS and spam, November 2005.
2004 · XP SP2: firewall on, DEP — Service Pack 2, August 2004.

2005 · IM worms: Bropia, Kelvir — Bropia (January 2005) sends itself as a .pif over MSN Messenger; Kelvir (March 2005) sends a link to it. MSN Messenger 7 blocks .pif and filters executable transfers on 7 April 2005; the links were not covered.
2005 · MSN Messenger 7 filters unsafe transfers — 7 April 2005: .pif messages blocked and executable transfers filtered, after Bropia and Kelvir; links were not covered.
2005 · Kernel Patch Protection (x64) — First shipped 2005 on XP x64 and Server 2003 SP1.
2005 · Botnets for hire: spam, DDoS, click fraud — Botnet capacity rented for spam and DDoS; browsers monetized by click fraud. The infected machine is inventory.

g.text: Botnets for hire: spam, DDoS, click fraud

circle.title: 2005 · Network IDS/IPS — Payload signatures on plaintext traffic.
2005 · Sony BMG rootkit — Disclosed by Mark Russinovich, 31 October 2005.
2006 · Flash, Java, Acrobat plug-ins — The browser exploitation surface of the decade.

2006 · Exploit documents, then MPack (2006–08) — A Word zero-day in targeted attacks, May 2006 (MS06-027); MPack, the first exploit kit sold commercially, documented May–June 2007; a PDF exploit in the wild with zero antivirus detections, November 2008 (CVE-2008-2992).
2006 · Rustock — Kernel rootkit and spam bot, first analysed June 2006.
2007 · Storm Worm — First large spam run 19 January 2007 (F-Secure; detection added 15 January); server-side polymorphism at scale.
2007 · Vista: UAC, signed drivers, ASLR — Consumer release 30 January 2007; mandatory 64-bit driver signing.
2007 · Server-side polymorphism — Thousands of unique variants per day; hashes become one-shot.
2007 · Banking trojans, carding — Credentials and cards become the product.
2007 · Zeus — Banking trojan first identified July 2007.
2007 · Mebroot MBR bootkit — First traces November 2007; drive-by waves December 2007 to January 2008.
2008 · Fake antivirus — Rogue AV scams peak 2008–2011.
2008 · Koobface — Detected 31 July 2008 on MySpace and Facebook: a social-network worm whose botnet earned over US$2 million from pay-per-install and click fraud between June 2009 and June 2010.
2008 · McAfee Artemis — Cloud reputation, announced September 2008.
2008 · Conficker — Conficker.A detected 21 November 2008.
2009 · Symantec Quorum / Insight — File prevalence in Norton 2010, announced September 2009.
2009 · Windows 7 ships PowerShell 2.0 — 22 October 2009: an interpreter on every machine.
2010 · State espionage and sabotage — A payoff that is strategic, not financial.
2010 · Operation Aurora — Disclosed by Google, 12 January 2010.
2010 · Stuxnet — Identified 17 June 2010.
2010 · Exploit-kit rental — Blackhole licensed by the year or rented by the day.
2010 · Blackhole exploit kit — Active roughly 2010–2013.

2010 · Facebook Messages: attachments, executables blocked — Launched 15 November 2010 with executables and batch files excluded; a renaming bypass published 27 October 2011, answered with antivirus scanning. Koobface had spread by link since 2008.
2011 · Kill chain paper — Hutchins, Cloppert and Amin, 2011.
2011 · Cuckoo Sandbox — First public beta 5 February 2011.
2011 · Mimikatz — First public release May 2011.
2011 · Office 365 — Launched 28 June 2011.
2011 · GameOver Zeus — Peer-to-peer Zeus variant from September 2011, after the Zeus source leak that May; banking fraud at scale until June 2014.
2011 · WildFire sandbox — Palo Alto Networks, November 2011.

2012 · Incident-response agents before the name — Mandiant's and Carbon Black's host agents recorded process and connection history for investigators; Gartner names the category in 2013 by listing them.
2012 · Police lockers (Reveton) — 2012: the screen is locked in the name of the police and a $100 fine is paid by prepaid money card; the extortion model before Bitcoin.
2012 · PowerSploit — May 2012.
2012 · Cobalt Strike — First release summer 2012.
2012 · Windows 8: Secure Boot, Defender antivirus built in — 26 October 2012: UEFI Secure Boot, and Windows Defender becomes a full antivirus on every machine.
2013 · APT1 report — Mandiant, 18 February 2013.

2013 · Snowden disclosures — From 6 June 2013. Encryption by default becomes the industry's answer and the IETF declares pervasive monitoring an attack (RFC 7258, May 2014): the cause of the HTTPS curve.
2013 · EDR named — Anton Chuvakin, Gartner, 26 July 2013: 'endpoint threat detection and response'.
2013 · Bitcoin ransom (CryptoLocker) — The victim pays the attacker directly, September 2013.
2013 · CryptoLocker — First seen about 5 September 2013.
2013 · FireEye IPO: sandbox peak — 20 September 2013.
2013 · Angler exploit kit — Late 2013 to June 2016.
2013 · Target POS breach — 27 November to 15 December 2013; about 40 million cards.
2014 · CylancePROTECT (ML on PE features) — 18 February 2014.
2014 · XP end of support — 8 April 2014.
2014 · GameOver Zeus takedown (Operation Tovar) — 2 June 2014: the leading banking-fraud botnet and the CryptoLocker infrastructure disrupted together.
2014 · Poweliks (registry-resident) — Disclosed 31 July 2014.
2014 · Sysmon — Sysinternals Sysmon 1.0, 5 August 2014.
2014 · Macros return (Dridex) — Word-macro delivery from late October 2014.
2015 · Chrome drops NPAPI plug-ins — Java plug-in disabled April 2015, removed September 2015.
2015 · ATT&CK public — May 2015; 96 techniques, 9 tactics.
2015 · Kovter goes fileless — Registry-resident variant, May 2015.
2015 · Windows 10: AMSI, script block logging — 29 July 2015; Device Guard and Credential Guard in Enterprise editions.
2015 · PowerShell Empire — BSides Las Vegas, 5 August 2015.
2015 · Let's Encrypt public beta — 3 December 2015; about 40 percent of Firefox page loads were HTTPS.
2015 · Ukraine grid attack — 23 December 2015: BlackEnergy for access, then operators by hand opening breakers at three utilities; the first confirmed cyber-induced outage.
2016 · Oracle deprecates Java plug-in — 27 January 2016.
2016 · Bangladesh Bank heist — 4–5 February 2016; attributed to North Korea.
2016 · Locky — First seen 16 February 2016.
2016 · Windows Defender ATP: EDR built into Windows 10 — Announced 1 March 2016, shipped with the Anniversary Update on 2 August 2016: post-breach detection as an operating-system feature.
2016 · Mirai botnet — Source published at the end of September 2016; the Dyn attack on 21 October 2016. Cameras and routers that can never run an agent: the edge arrives as a botnet.
2016 · HTTPS passes half of page loads — Firefox 50 percent on 13 October 2016; Chrome on Windows about 51 percent.
2017 · Shadow Brokers leak — EternalBlue published 14 April 2017.
2017 · BEC top IC3 loss category — Largest reported loss category every year 2017–2021; overtaken by investment fraud in 2022.
2017 · WannaCry — 12 May 2017.
2017 · JA3 TLS fingerprinting — Salesforce, June 2017.
2017 · NotPetya — 27 June 2017; attributed to the Russian military 15 February 2018.
2017 · CCleaner supply chain — Disclosed 18 September 2017.
2017 · ASR rules (Windows 10 1709) — Exploit Guard, October 2017.
2018 · Cryptojacking — Monero mining in browsers and on servers.
2018 · EDR mainstream; XDR — Detection moves to the host; managed detection and response. XDR as a product from Cortex XDR, February 2019.
2018 · Chrome marks HTTP 'Not secure' — Chrome 68, 24 July 2018.
2018 · Big-game ransomware — Ryuk from August 2018: the organization pays directly.
2018 · Emotet, TrickBot, Ryuk — The 2018–2019 loader-to-ransomware chain.
2018 · TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) — August 2018: the server certificate is encrypted.
2018 · DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484) — October 2018.
2018 · ATT&CK Evaluations, round 1 (APT3) — Results published November 2018: EDR products measured technique by technique against one emulated adversary.

2019 · Malware-free intrusions pass half — CrowdStrike's yearly reports: malware-free detections 40 percent in 2018, 51 percent in 2019, 62 percent at the end of 2021, 79 percent in 2024. PowerShell, WMI, living-off-the-land binaries, Cobalt Strike, DLL side-loading, memory-only implants.
2019 · Defender tamper protection — GA 14 October 2019.
2019 · Double extortion (Maze) — Allied Universal leak threat, November 2019.
2020 · Citrix ADC and Pulse Secure VPN exploited — CVE-2019-19781 (disclosed December 2019) and CVE-2019-11510 (2019): edge appliances become an entry point before any host is touched.
2020 · Windows 7 end of support — 14 January 2020.
2020 · Firefox DoH default (US) — 25 February 2020.
2020 · Remote work; identity is the perimeter — Cloud-first, OAuth tokens, SaaS everywhere.

g.text: Remote work; identity is the perimeter

circle.title: 2020 · Initial-access brokers, infostealer logs — Access itself becomes the traded commodity.
2020 · NIST SP 800-207 zero trust — 11 August 2020.
2020 · SolarWinds — SUNBURST disclosed 13 December 2020.
2020 · Flash end of life — 31 December 2020: the exploit kits' favourite target is gone.
2021 · ProxyLogon — 2 March 2021.
2021 · Chrome on Windows passes 90% HTTPS — April 2021.
2021 · Colonial Pipeline (DarkSide) — 7 May 2021: the pipeline shut down for days; about 75 bitcoin paid, most of it seized by the DOJ in June.

2021 · FireEye sells its products business — 2 June 2021, to Symphony Technology Group for $1.2 billion; VMware had bought Lastline in June 2020. The bookend to the 2013 IPO: the sandbox is a bundled feature now.
2021 · Kaseya — 2 July 2021.
2021 · Windows 11: TPM 2.0, VBS default — 5 October 2021; virtualization-based security (VBS) on by default for new installs.

2021 · Implants in Go and Rust (BlackCat) — BlackCat, the first major ransomware written in Rust, mid-November 2021; Go malware had multiplied through 2020. Still PE files, but each runtime needs its own unpacking, symbol recovery and decompilation.
2021 · Log4Shell — 9 December 2021.
2022 · State cryptocurrency heists — North Korean theft at scale.
2022 · Wipers in Ukraine; Viasat — HermeticWiper on 23 February 2022; KA-SAT modems bricked on 24 February: state sabotage at the start of the invasion.
2022 · ITDR named (Gartner) — 7 March 2022.
2022 · LAPSUS$ — Okta, Microsoft, Nvidia, early 2022: help desks and MFA fatigue.
2022 · Internet macros blocked — Announced February, rolled out July 2022.
2022 · Driver blocklist on by default — Windows 11 22H2, 20 September 2022.
2022 · Smart App Control — Windows 11 22H2, September 2022.
2022 · BYOVD EDR killers — Bring your own vulnerable driver: a signed, exploitable driver loaded to switch the EDR off from the kernel. BlackByte, Lazarus, Cuba, 2022.
2023 · AI assistants in browsers, IDEs, SaaS — Copilots everywhere.

g.text: AI assistants in browsers, IDEs, SaaS

circle.title: 2023 · LSA protection default (enterprise) — New enterprise-joined installs, 22H2 and later.
2023 · Volt Typhoon advisory — CISA AA23-144A, 24 May 2023: living off the land as the whole campaign.
2023 · Extortion without encryption — Cl0p and MOVEit, May–June 2023.
2023 · State prepositioning — Volt Typhoon: not paid at all.
2023 · Cl0p MOVEit — Exploitation from about 27 May 2023.
2023 · Identity threat detection and response — The sensor moves to the identity provider.
2023 · Scattered Spider: MGM, Caesars — September 2023; help-desk calls and MFA resets.
2023 · Help-desk SE against casinos — Payout justifies live social engineering.
2023 · ECH in Chrome and Firefox — September–October 2023; Cloudflare default for free zones.
2023 · Passkeys in Windows 11 — September 2023.
2023 · Citrix Bleed — CVE-2023-4966, October 2023.

2023 · Collaboration tools as the new mail — Storm-0324 phishes through Teams with SharePoint-hosted files (Microsoft, 12 September 2023); Black Basta's fake help-desk Teams calls from May 2024; Discord's content network hosted payloads until it moved to expiring links, November 2023.

2024 · Edge devices: Citrix Bleed, Ivanti, Fortinet — Citrix Bleed October 2023, Ivanti Connect Secure zero-days January 2024, Fortinet SSL-VPN February 2024: appliances that run no EDR become the main entry point.
2024 · CISA LOTL guidance; baselining — 7 February 2024.
2024 · Fortinet SSL-VPN — CVE-2024-21762, February 2024.
2024 · Session tokens as the product — A token opens the SaaS tenant where the data lives.
2024 · XZ Utils backdoor — Found 29 March 2024: a maintainer identity built over two years to plant a backdoor in a Linux compression library on the path to SSH.
2024 · ClickFix — The user pastes the command; first observed March 2024.
2024 · Snowflake customer breaches — May–June 2024: infostealer credentials with no MFA opened about 165 customer tenants; data stolen and extorted without touching a host.

2024 · CrowdStrike outage; EDR out of the kernel — 19 July 2024: a faulty sensor update crashed about 8.5 million Windows hosts. Microsoft's Windows Resiliency Initiative (November 2024) moves endpoint security out of kernel mode.
2024 · LLM triage in the SOC — Reasoning applied on the defensive side.

2024 · Salt Typhoon (telecoms) — Disclosed September–November 2024: a state actor inside carrier networks, reaching call records and data held for court-ordered law-enforcement requests; in through edge equipment.
2024 · Agent protocols (MCP) — Tool-using agents become products.
2025 · Bybit heist (North Korea) — 21 February 2025: about $1.5 billion in cryptocurrency, the largest theft on record; FBI attribution on 26 February.

2025 · Firmware botnets in consumer devices — BADBOX (identified 2023) and BADBOX 2.0 (FBI warning, 5 June 2025): Android TV boxes and other devices backdoored before purchase. XCPE, disclosed 2 November 2026: the backdoor in the manufacturer's own firmware on more than 1.3 million set-top boxes.
2025 · Project Ire — Microsoft, 5 August 2025: agentic malware analysis.
2025 · ForcedLeak (hijacked agent) — Noma Security, 25 September 2025.
2025 · Windows 10 end of support — 14 October 2025.

2025 · AI-orchestrated espionage campaign reported — Anthropic, 13 November 2025: a state-linked operator had an agent run most of an intrusion campaign; agent-assisted extortion had been reported in August 2025.
2025 · Guardrails, agent observability — The sensor moves into the agent harness.
2026 · ECH standardized (RFC 9849) — March 2026; server-side adoption still narrow.

2026 · ATT&CK adds Defense Impairment — ATT&CK v19, 28 April 2026: Defense Evasion split into Stealth and Defense Impairment. v20, 13 October 2026, adds Impair Autonomous Defenses, including prompt injection against LLM-assisted analysis (slide 16).
2026 · Autonomous agent intrusion — Hugging Face technical timeline of the July 2026 incident.

2026 · File-based implants persist: NIK C2, VOLTA — Talos, October 2026: NIK C2, a Go remote-access tool with an OpenAI client; VOLTA, a built-to-order infostealer that sends the stolen bundle to an LLM to rank the victim's assets. Still PE files for sale.

2026 · Bandwidth as the product again — XCPE, disclosed 2 November 2026: a device manufacturer sells access to more than 1.3 million set-top boxes to affiliates for residential proxies and ad fraud. The botnet-for-hire model of 2005, on devices no one patches.

2026 · Browser-resident C2 (Falcon/XG) — Unit 42, 11 November 2026: the implant is JavaScript in a browser tab or a sideloaded extension, no host file; a tab injection is scoped to one site, an extension hijacks the whole browser. The same actor drops a native Rust implant (Antino) via a fake Adobe Flash update.
